subject: pirateGalleon
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: pirate galleon under full sail.
Style: your choice. Pick an unexpected, striking visual style that suits this subject (not the obvious one), name it in a comment at the top of the module, and commit to it everywhere.
reasoning:
I'm brainstorming unexpected stylistic approaches for the galleon — considering woodcut nautical engravings, ukiyo-e, papercraft dioramas, and settling on an intriguing idea: rendering the ship as blue-and-white Delft porcelain with glazed ceramic texture.

I'm committing to a strict palette of white, pale blue, cobalt, and deep indigo, with maybe tiny gold-lustre accents on fittings like cannons, keeping it disciplined like real Delftware pieces. For scale, I'm aiming for a realistic galleon size — roughly 36 meters long with tall masts — and planning the module to be substantial but manageable, around 500-700 lines, written carefully since I can't test-run it.

I'm deciding the hull keel sits flush at y=0 without any separate base or wave platform, letting the rounded hull bottom rest on that line like a keel beam. Since this is a static, non-rigged model, I'm opting to skip joints entirely and keep all geometry in model space under the untagged root group for simplicity.

For the hull itself, rather than relying on uncertain loft section defaults, I'm planning to manually construct the lofted hull shape from custom cross-section stations along the length, building the buffer geometry myself to have full control over the profile.

I'm defining the hull cross-section profile at each station, with points running from the keel up through the bilge to the gunwale, incorporating a tumblehome shape so the hull narrows near the top like a galleon. Then I'll connect these profile points across stations with quad strips to build the hull surface.

I'm also planning the deck as a separate flat mesh fitted between the gunwales, plus bulwark rails, a flat stern transom closing off one end, and a bow that tapers to a point at the other. Beyond the basic hull, I want raised structures like the aftercastle and forecastle built from boxes with painted window details, and a Delft-style paint scheme with blue planking lines, a cobalt wale stripe, and wavy borders over white glaze.

For the gunports, I'm figuring out how to place small dark-blue box decals directly on the hull surface by interpolating a profile function that gives x and y at any given z, then offsetting each port slightly outward so it sits embedded in the hull.

Simplifying further, I decide ports will just be flat deep-blue boxes with a white lid box above, plus tiny cobalt cylinders as protruding cannon muzzles. Now I'm settling on a limited color palette—white and glaze tones, cobalt blue, and a deeper navy—keeping the total flat colors under 64 since paint textures don't count against that limit.

I'm sticking strictly to blue-and-white Delft tones, skipping gold or red accents, and fixing porcelain gloss roughness at 0.72. For the sails, I'm planning custom curved geometry—a grid patch that bulges forward to look billowed by wind, wider at the bottom, with UV mapping for texture detail.

For the sail texture itself, I want painted Delft-style motifs like cobalt skull-and-crossbones with scrollwork and floral tile-corner borders, and since textures only render front-facing, I need the sail geometry to have proper double-sided surfaces—building front and back layers with mirrored UVs and slight thickness so normals read correctly on both sides.

I'm making sure the SVG background is fully opaque white so transparent pixels don't cut through the sail, keeping the drawing simple enough that mirrored text/symbols still read fine from the back. Now I'm designing a parametric sail geometry function controlling top/bottom width, height, belly curve, and segment resolution.

Writing geometry function...

Now I'm planning the mast layout—foremast, mainmast, mizzen with lateen, and bowsprit with spritsail—setting their positions and heights with tiered courses, topsails, and topgallants rising from the deck.

For yards and masts I'll use a tapered rod helper to connect endpoints with varying radius, applying striped paint patterns for a ceramic banded look on the masts.

For rigging, I'm weighing options: individual rod shrouds from masthead to gunwale chains versus rendering ratlines as flat double-sided textured cards showing a ladder-net pattern, since many thin parts could balloon the part count.

Settling on the texture-card approach: a double-sided quad with a transparent SVG texture showing shroud lines and ratlines, using alphaTest so the empty areas vanish — cheap and visually convincing compared to modeling every rope segment.

Placing without a bone should be fine since static builder geometry stays in model space under the root. I should plan the texture set carefully: distinct sail textures (main course, fore, topsail, topgallant, lateen, spritsail), plus flag, shroud ladder, stern windows, stern plaque, and maybe a figurehead — keeping shared textures per material to avoid bloat.

Now I'm sketching the Delft-style sail designs: cobalt-and-white tile motifs with repeating spiral/lozenge borders and a central medallion, like a skull-and-crossbones wreathed in laurel with fleur corner accents. I'm defining a color palette (cobalt, mid-blue, pale blue, white) and starting to build the SVG for the main sail with a wide aspect ratio and a white background base.

Writing SVG code...

For corner ornaments I'm planning small quarter-circle fan curls at each corner using arc paths, and double-checking the sail billow direction matches the ship facing forward with square sails hanging in the x-y plane.

Now I'm working through the texture orientation on the sail—figuring out whether +X maps to the viewer's left or right when looking at the bow from the front, using a cross product to nail down the correct handedness.

Moving on to the yards: I'm positioning tapered rods along the x-axis at various heights to form the horizontal spars, placing them slightly forward of the mast so the sails can hang with their proper belly curve.

Now I'm structuring each mast's tiers—course, topsail, topgallant—with tapered mast segments, and building a lathed crow's nest platform for the main mast using a profile outline.

Writing yardarm and flag details...

Working out triangle winding...

Working out the flag orientation math confirms the normal points correctly toward +x, so the texture mapping will read properly for viewers on that side. For the design, I'll go with a deep blue Delft field with a white skull-and-bones emblem to keep it bold and legible, and I'm considering using transparency in the pennant texture to create the triangular cut shape.

For the hull, I'm planning layered paint details: horizontal plank lines in pale blue, slightly tinted strakes, cobalt wale stripes, and a wavy scroll-pattern border band near the waterline. Below the waterline I'll switch to a deep blue fish-scale pattern to suggest antifouling paint.

Now I'm sketching out the ship's dimensions: length running from stern at z=-15 to bow near z=+15, with a beakhead and bowsprit extending to z=+25, a beam of about 9.2 total, and figuring out how the keel and waterline heights relate for the floating depth.

I'm defining the half-beam curve across stations from stern to bow, narrower at the stern, widest around 40% of the length, then tapering sharply to a point at the bow.

Now I'm shaping the keel line, rising near the bow and stern while staying flat at the midship, and setting the deck sheer curve with its height at the stern, midship, and bow before handling the stern castle separately.

I'll build the decks as separate flat boxes sized to the hull width at each section—main deck, quarterdeck, and forecastle—each positioned at different heights, with the bulwark walls continuing upward above them.

I could paint the interior faces a pale Delft blue by checking whether the normal points inward relative to the hull's centerline, giving that lived-in painted look. Then I'll add a gunwale rail as a swept shape following the hull's top edge curve, using a tapered elliptical cross-section in deep blue to cap the rim.

Decks need to sit below this gunwale line with enough interior wall height to feel enclosed, and the hull's double-sided, closed-bottom construction should hide any gaps. For the stern, I still need a separate transom face closing off the back—built as a flat fan panel at that station so I can later add the painted plaque and stern gallery detail.

I'm adding a stern gallery overhang with window planes, balcony rails, and three tall lantern posts for that classic galleon look, then moving to the beakhead—running a bowsprit rod forward from the bow and shaping a cutwater wedge to connect it to the hull.

For the figurehead, I'm sketching a simple ceramic dragon or lion-like head using basic primitives: a cone snout, cobalt sphere eyes, a lower jaw, and a ring of alternating cobalt/white spike cones forming a mane, mounted just below the bowsprit at the bow.

I'll also add deck details: cobalt cylinder cannon barrels with white wheels, gun ports along the hull, and an anchor shape near the bow.

I'm planning a ship's wheel from a ring of rods for spokes at the quarterdeck, plus barrels, crates, a Jolly Roger flag, bell, crow's nests, ratlines, lanterns, a rudder, and maybe a small scaled sphere for a longboat on deck. I also want to add a Delft-style motif to the side gun ports for a decorative touch.

For the hull resting position, I'm deciding to skip a visible ground and instead add a slight keel beam at the bottom so the ship doesn't look like it's floating without support, keeping texture and triangle budgets in check before starting the actual build code.

Setting up imports and core builder utilities...

I'm figuring out texel density for the galleon's hull paint texture — with a hull area around 2000 m² and a 2048 paint size, I get roughly 2.6 cm per texel, so plank lines need to be at least 0.06 wide to render clearly rather than collapsing into a single texel.

Now I'm writing the hull geometry function, defining beam width and keel curves as functions of position along the hull length to shape the bow and stern tapering.

With gunwale aft at 9.9 and bow at 9.6, I'm laying out the waist deck lower at 5.6, plus separate quarterdeck and forecastle platforms near their respective gunwale heights, stepping between them as boxes across the appropriate z-ranges.

Now I'm defining the hull cross-section profile at each station, working out a series of normalized points along the beam and height that trace the rounded bottom, flaring sides, and tumblehome curve up to the gunwale, including a wale bump near the top before narrowing inward.

Defining hull profile points...

Still working out the vertex ordering...

At the bow I'll leave a small flat cap plate since the width there is near-zero anyway, covered by the figurehead; similarly the stern needs a closing fan of triangles around a center point, and I need to work out the correct winding order by checking viewer orientation looking from behind the stern.

So (c, p_k, p_{k+1}) works for the bow cap normal. For double-sided interior rendering, I'll add a reversed inner copy of the hull so the interior shows as pale blue, determining "inside" by checking whether the normal points toward or away from the central axis rather than duplicating exact geometry.

Caps give a zero dot product with the radial vector so they default to exterior treatment, which is acceptable since cap interiors just get the same paint anyway, and the keel line stays shared between bottom surfaces. With flat shading and roughly 14 stations by 12 columns I'd get around 700 low-poly triangles for a chunky ceramic-faceted look, though bumping up to 18 stations should smooth that out a bit.

I'm also wondering whether the paint baking needs UV coordinates on the geometry, since without them it's unclear how the SDK would atlas the texture — safest bet is to just add a simple unique UV layout (u from the ring parameter, v from ring index) to avoid any overlapping-chart issues during the bake.

I'll give caps their own planar uv and just supply uv universally even if unused, since textured atlas tiles don't rely on paint bake. Moving on to deck geometry, starting with the main waist deck as a thin box spanning the hull's midsection.

For the decks, I need a generic strip-building function that follows the hull's side curve at a given y-height, drawing only the top surface since the hull hides the underside, then painting it with alternating plank-colored stripes along z. Still writing deck strip logic...

I'm also adding vertical bulkhead walls at the deck boundaries with door/window textures, plus a poop deck above the quarterdeck near the stern, built as a small enclosed cabin box supported by walls.

Now I'm working out the geometry helper functions: one to find the hull's side profile x-position at a given height by interpolating between control points, and another to build deck strips as paneled grids with correct front-facing normals across each station.

Each gridGeo part gets unique uv for painting, so deck planks get a line pattern based on position with alternating plank tints, and hull/deck parts stay separate with their own coordinates. Now I'm thinking about rails: adding simple rod rails along deck edges and balustrades near the quarterdeck and poop front, keeping the geometry modest.

I'm designing a balustrade helper that builds a rail rod with evenly spaced posts, and planning a gunwale cap as a swept path following the hull's top edge with an elliptical cross-section using a tapered box radius function.

I'm adding painted rope-like dashes along the sweep using striped blue-and-white coloring banded across the path, and closing off the stern rail with a rod spanning the transom at gunwale height. Now I'm thinking through adding raised wale bands as protruding sweeps along the hull sides.

I'm placing 2-3 wale bands at specific heights, following the sheer line upward toward bow and stern using fractional interpolation of hull height rather than fixed y-values, which should give a more characteristic curved look.

So the box extents give x-thickness for protrusion and ry for vertical height, with the centerline offset from the side. For the hull paint, I realize it should compute its own frac value from position rather than relying on raw y, deriving yk and H at that z to get a sheer-following coordinate. Then I'm planning the paint zones by frac: below f<0.28 I'll put a cobalt fish-scale pattern against white.

Working out the staggered scale grid math...

Adding deep band and plank line patterns between wales, plus a decorative diamond motif band.

I want to add slight wobble to the paint lines by jittering f with noise, giving it a hand-painted Delft feel, and reuse the hull paint for cap areas since they're mostly hidden by the gallery. For interior planking I'll mix white with glaze lines, then move on to placing the gun ports -- trying to fit them into the band between the wale stripes without clashing with the diamond pattern there.

Reworking the vertical zones: a thin cobalt wale around f 0.42-0.48 and a deeper one at 0.80-0.86, with white planking between holding the gun ports around f=0.62, diamonds along the bulwark top at 0.86-0.94, and a blue stripe capping it off at 0.94-1. I'm now stepping through port positions along t to decide their horizontal spacing.

I need to check the frame protrudes slightly more than the inner dark panel, sharing the same center, and confirm the port placement stays within valid t-range near the bow curve and below the forecastle/quarterdeck height limits.

For the cannons, I'm planning to add cylindrical barrels poking outward from each port using a rod shape, mirrored across both sides with a sign flip on x. I also need a tapered rudder box behind the stern, then I'm starting to define the mast data structure for the rigging.

Working out the mast placements now: foremast near the bow around z=6, mainmast near midship, mizzen on the quarterdeck toward the stern, each with staged heights for lower mast and topmast sections with tapering radii.

I'm figuring out yard dimensions and sail placements for the course and topsail — spans, heights, and vertical positions along each mast to get the proportions right.

Then I'm working through the mast heights, platform positions, and yard lengths for the main mast tops before moving to the fore mast's lower yard, sail foot height, and clearance above the forecastle deck.

Continuing with topsail and topgallant yard heights, finishing the fore mast at height 29.5, then I want to formalize the sail tiers systematically with yard height, sail height, top/bottom width, texture and belly for each mast. For the mizzen I'm planning a lateen sail with a long diagonal yard running from low forward to high aft, on a 22-unit mast.

Working out triangle parametrization...

Now I'm thinking through how to add a belly curve to the sail shape using sine offsets along both axes, keeping edges flat and the apex pinched to zero, then moving on to positioning the spritsail under the bowsprit.

For the spritsail I'm placing the yard at z≈19.5 on the bowsprit, letting the sail hang down with forward belly, and then setting up the jib staysails as triangular shapes stretched between the bowsprit tip and the foremast heads, reusing a generic three-point grid function to give them sideways belly.

I'm generalizing this into a triSail function taking luff edge points and an apex, with belly direction as a parameter, so I can reuse it for the lateen and jibs alike. For textures I'm planning a full set covering twelve sail/decoration types—main, fore, top, gallant, lateen, jib, sprit, flag, pennant, shroud, window, and stern plaque—each as compact SVG patterns to keep within budget.

Now I'm working out the UV mapping for the triangular lateen sail, since the width collapses to a point at the apex: I'm defining texture coordinates along the yard versus toward the apex, then computing where the centroid lands in that space so I can place a compass-rose motif there correctly.

For shrouds I'm building a ladder shape with quad geometry stretching from the hull chains up to the mast top, using a simple ratline texture that naturally narrows toward the apex. Each mast gets a pair of shrouds per side, six total, with lower sections running chains-to-platform and upper sections platform-to-topmast.

I'm also adding stays connecting mastheads with thin faceted rod geometry, lathe-built top platforms and a crow's nest barrel on the main topmast, plus flags: a Jolly Roger trailing off the main top, smaller pennants on fore and mizzen, and a stern ensign on the poop deck.

For the stern, I'm designing a transom with a gallery and a decorative oval plaque depicting a miniature galleon scene, mounted on the back wall of the poop cabin, with dimensions for the cabin box and transom width worked out to match the hull's beam proportions.

I'm checking that the poop cabin fits within the hull's narrowing stern profile, computing half-widths at various z positions to ensure the cabin walls stay inside the bulwark line while extending slightly above it, then sizing the cabin walls with white paint and blue paneling plus window details.

Now I'm adding the roof structure sized slightly larger than the cabin with corner lanterns and a balustrade, then working out a stern gallery bump near the transom—figuring out its box dimensions and position so it hugs the hull curvature without clipping outside, plus placing window planes on its back face.

I'm then puzzling over the plaque placement: the stern view is secondary, so rather than overcomplicate the gallery, I'm considering just mounting the plaque directly on the cabin's back wall where it rises above the bulwark line.

Mizzen top sits around 24-25, geometry checks out overall. Now I'm working out the forecastle structure: a riser wall at the bow bulkhead with door detailing, and a matching quarterdeck riser toward the stern.

For the door texture I decide to skip a separate asset and just reuse the window texture for both the riser panels and cabin windows, keeping the total texture count manageable around 12-13. I'm also planning a simple paint pattern of white with blue diamond panels for the riser walls, derived from position coordinates for consistency.

For lighting, I'll bring in the glow kit for lanterns, giving them a cold blue-white light with strength 1.2 and color "#dff0ff" to fit the blue/white palette. Now I'm turning to deck props — thinking I'll skip extra cannons but add a longboat amidships on the main deck, shaping its hull from a scaled half-ellipsoid sphere geometry.

Working out the boat's shape...

I'll skip the longboat entirely and lean on barrels and hatch gratings for detail instead. Now I'm setting up the builder with a name and paint size, then writing a helper function for grid-based geometry generation...

Writing grid geometry helper...

I'm weighing whether `flat:true` suits sails versus decks, and realizing parts without a bone or joint need somewhere to attach — maybe safest to add a single root joint like "ship" at the origin so every part has a valid rigid attachment, even for static models.

Deciding to skip joints since static models work fine in model space. Now I'm setting up color constants and a wreath-drawing helper that generates leaf shapes in SVG for ornamental corners.

Writing skull and crossbones SVG...

Still drawing the skull details...

Now I'm setting up the sail's main SVG with a border, seam lines, and dashed reef bands, making sure the bones layer behind the skull with knobbed ends.

Placing fan ornaments at the four inner-border corners...

Now I'm checking the sail's aspect ratio against the viewBox stretch—the main course sail is roughly 2.1:1, so I'm adjusting the viewBox dimensions to match that proportion so circular medallions stay round rather than stretched.

I'll build a parametric sail texture function that takes width, height, and a center art generator, then composes a border, seams, corner ornaments, and a medallion circle sized relative to the sail dimensions, with raster output at 512px.

For each mast I need distinct central emblems — skull for the main sail, an anchor built from shank/ring/stock/arms for the fore sail, a little galleon with masts and triangular sails for the topsail, a Delft-style tulip with petals and stem leaves for the topgallant, and I'm considering a compass star, laurel wreath, or sun-with-rays motif for the lateen and spritsail.

Now I'm turning to the window texture: an arched shape painted in deep indigo with a white mullion cross and pale glass panes, framed in blue with a diamond lattice pattern to give it that stained-glass church window feel.

I'm also planning the plaque texture as an oval frame with a double blue outline and leaf motifs, containing a galleon illustration riding waves, plus the flag texture using a deep base color and a skull emblem.

For the skull I'm parametrizing a reusable function with center, scale, and color inputs so bones and skull can take white fills with dark eyes for the flag version, and for the pennant I'm sketching a swallowtail path shape striped with blue and white, possibly via a clip path.

I'll simplify by drawing the pennant path in solid blue then layering white dots or dashes along the centerline on top rather than clipping. For multiple pennant colors I'll just invert fill and stroke rather than building separate textures, and I'm noting shrouds stay transparent background while sails reuse the same texture front and back. I'm also confirming shape-rendering settings and accepting that repeated loop-generated textures will produce long strings, then moving on to work out actual geometry placements.

Writing hull profile functions...

I'm noticing the keel bottoms out to a flat ridge at y=0 across the midship section, so now I'm building the outer hull geometry function that generates rings of vertices along the hull profile.

Still writing hull mesh code...

Working out the cap triangulation...

Still writing hull paint logic...

Still defining color bands...

Adding plank patterns for the hull, interior, and deck surfaces...

Checking the other deck ranges confirms the geometry works at the quarterdeck too, and I verify the deck's winding order produces an upward-facing normal using the cross product of the u and v directions.

For the risers, I'm computing box positions for the stair steps between deck levels, sizing them by the side-width function at each step. For the forecastle, I'm placing a riser box and adding window planes on the aft-facing wall toward the waist, offsetting them in z and orienting them opposite the quarterdeck's windows since the default plane geometry faces +Z.

Now I'm working out the bowsprit and beakhead: a tapered rod running forward and up from the bow, plus a curved cutwater sweep built from a catmull spline with tapering radius, painted blue, positioned just below the bowsprit near the bow tip.

Checking the geometry, the lion head figurehead sits at the end of the beakhead sweep, facing forward and tilted slightly upward, positioned just under the bowsprit line so they don't overlap. I'm building the head as a flattened white sphere with a mane made of twelve spikes ringed around the front-facing axis.

Now I'm working out the mane detail with two overlapping rings of spikes at different radii, alternating colors, and offset angles so they interleave rather than stack directly on top of each other.

Actually tilt should be negative so the mane flares backward, away from the forward line direction, giving a swept-back look. I'll add the muzzle box, cobalt eye spheres, nose, jaw, teeth, and small ear spheres as the remaining head details, keeping the part count modest.

Now I'm moving to the masts, writing a function that builds segmented rods with porcelain spiral paint banding for decoration.

Writing mast geometry...

Adding crosstrees and small topmast-head rods, then working out a generalized per-mast formula with base, lower-top, topmast, and topgallant heights. For the fore and main masts I'm pinning down yard heights—course yard, topsail yard, and topgallant yard—checking they line up correctly against each platform and mast segment.

Now I'm sanity-checking the sail geometry: course sail foot versus deck and bulwark height, then topsail yard and foot positions against the main top platform's radius and z-range to catch any overlap. I'm spotting a clash where the topsail foot intersects the platform disc, so I'm nudging the topsail foot upward above the platform and adjusting the yard height accordingly to keep it realistic.

I'm now working through the same yard/foot/height calculations for the topgallant, fore mast, and mizzen mast sails, checking each against its respective platform and topmast range to make sure nothing collides and the proportions stay consistent across all three masts.

Clearing cabin roof height of 13.5 should sit fine, with the triangle A(-2.6,11.6), B(-13.4,22.2), C(-14.5,15.0) checking out—the foot line from A to C passes above cabin1's roof at roughly y≈13.2 near z=-8.

Checking cabin2 next: the clearance there also holds, with y≈14.3 at z=-12 beating the 13.5 roof line comfortably. I'm also confirming the mizzen mast and yard clearances work geometrically, then moving on to position the jibs using the bowsprit tip and fore topmast head as stay points.

Verifying the jib triangle: with luff running from A to B and clew at C, I check that the luff clears the bowsprit and spritsail at z=19.5, finding it comfortably above. Setting up the inner jib's tack point on the bowsprit and starting its head position next.

I'm checking whether jib1's foot line and jib2's luff line actually cross given their endpoint coordinates, comparing the y-values at matching z positions to confirm no overlap between the two sail triangles.

Jib2's luff at that height clears jib1's foot, so no overlap there. I'm also confirming jib texture sharing and belly sign conventions, then writing a helper function that builds a square sail's geometry, interpolating width from foot to head and adding a sideways belly bulge.

Working out the belly curve formula...

Settling on a power-of-sine curve for the sail's belly shape that tapers to zero at both the yard and foot, with the foot left as a straight line between clews, and adding a slight inward pinch near the bottom corners for a more natural sail silhouette.

Still refining sail curve math...

Positioning yards relative to masts and adding parrel boxes, then working out shroud geometry as quads running from chainwale points on the gunwale up to the mast, calculating the hull-width taper at those z-positions to place the bottom corners correctly.

I need alpha testing for the textured quads to cut out the transparent parts. Upper shrouds run from the platform rim up to the topmast head using a shorter version of the same ladder texture, and stays are thin rods connecting the mast tops. I still need to add flags, pennants, and a small rail around the crow's nest platform.

For the crow's nest itself, I'm working out a lathe shape to form a ring-like barrel shell, positioning it on the main topmast near the top, and shaping the outline carefully so the surfaces don't self-intersect.

Checking the crow's nest placement against the topgallant sail's position, I'm finding they'd overlap at that height. I'll skip the nest barrel entirely and rely on a simpler platform near the lower mast top instead.

Now I'm sketching an anchor hanging from the cathead near the bow, built from a shank, a crossbar stock, and two curved arms ending in small conical flukes. I'm also planning the ship's wheel at the quarterdeck as a vertical spoked disc facing aft.

Writing wheel geometry...

Now I'm planning the deck details: barrels with striped paint placed on the main deck and forecastle, quarterdeck cannons, a capstan built from cylinder and lathe shapes, and a hatch grate made from a box with striped lattice paint. I'm also adding stern lanterns mounted on the cabin roof.

I'm building hexagonal lantern shapes with a lathe base, glowing glass cylinder, cone cap, and finial sphere, placing two at the stern corners and one larger central lantern above the cabin. I'm aiming to keep the whole module in the 700-1100 line range, so I'm writing dense but careful code to hit that target before moving on to the rigging lines.

Now I'm sweeping the gunwale rail along both sides using a Catmull path derived from the hull's side curve, with a flat-capped boxed profile painted in the rail color, making sure the rail meets cleanly at the bow. I'm also setting up the wale sweep along a fixed hull fraction, working out how it should trace across the full length without conflicting with the keel.

Hull paint bands around f=0.42–0.48 line up with where the wale sweep sits, so they stay consistent. For the ports at f=0.62, I'm checking the box height of 0.9m against the hull's varying H to get the right f-range, roughly 0.13 in f-terms.

Working through the port positions along t from 0.21 to 0.74, I'm adjusting the gun's bulge using a smoothstep so it reads about 7.1 at t=0.74, and spacing out eight ports at 0.07 intervals starting from t=0.24.

Now I'm laying out the cannon barrels as rods with muzzle rings, deciding to skip the open lid detail for simplicity and instead frame each port with blue outer and indigo inner coloring.

I'm placing the stern gallery: a painted wall box, three window planes spaced along x at the transom, plus roof and floor ledges above and below, and I'm working out the hull's half-width at that height to size the gallery correctly.

Now I'm sizing cabin1, centering it between the quarterdeck and checking that its width stays inside the hull's inner bulwark line at that z-position, which means trimming the cabin's half-width slightly to fit the tapering hull.

I'm also catching that the cabin's back wall sticks past the hull's stern cap, so I'm pulling it flush at z=-15.0 and resizing depth accordingly, then placing the back windows so they sit above the bulwark rail without getting swallowed by it.

For the front face of the cabin, facing the open quarter deck, I'm putting two windows plus a centered door using the same window texture scaled taller. Now I'm moving on to block out the second cabin's position.

Now placing lantern poles at the roof corners plus a big lantern on cabin2's roof, then positioning the mizzen mast and checking the quarterdeck boundaries for conflicts. I'm adding balustrade rails with posts along the quarterdeck and forecastle edges, relying on the hull bulwark for the side rails.

Next I'm detailing the bowsprit rigging - gammoning lashings, the spritsail yard attached partway up the bowsprit with its sail dimensions and belly curve, and a small sprit mast rising above the bowsprit tip.

Now I'm skipping the bobstay for simplicity and moving to the standing rigging rods, connecting the mast tops to the bowsprit and each other using thin tapered rods with appropriate colors and segment counts.

Then I'm designing a function to generate wavy flags using a grid geometry, offsetting points sinusoidally along the length to create a rippling cloth effect with a pole-attached edge and a tapering pennant tail.

Writing skull SVG markup...

Still writing skull and eye details...

Still drawing ship hull, mast, sails, and wave pattern...

Now I'm sketching helper functions for other icons—a tulip with petals, stem, and leaves, a sun with rays, and starting a compass shape.

Then I'm building a reusable sail texture function that places diamond-shaped stitching marks and seam lines across the fabric, parameterized by width, height, and an art-drawing callback for the centerpiece.

I'm placing dashed reef bands horizontally so they get covered by the medallion, sizing corner fans relative to height, and working out proportions so strokes stay at least 3px when rendered at 512px. I'm calculating the medallion radius as a fraction of the smaller viewBox dimension.
